case: State of Odisha and Others v. Dhanurdhar Champatiray
headline: A Writ Petition Remains Available Against a Section 37 Arbitration Order Despite the Bar on Second Appeal: Orissa High Court
summary: Rejecting the preliminary objection that nine writ petitions against District Judges' Section 37 appellate orders were an impermissible substitute for a barred second appeal, Justice B.P. Routray held that the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 is not an appellate remedy and cannot be curtailed by the Arbitration Act's bar on second appeals, though such supervisory jurisdiction remain

case: ABC Constructions Pvt. Ltd. v. State Trading Corporation
headline: Interest Awarded 'From the Date of Cause of Action' Cannot Exceed What Section 31(7) Actually Permits: Delhi HC
summary: In a Section 34 challenge, the Delhi High Court partly set aside an arbitral award's interest component, holding that a tribunal awarding pendente lite and post-award interest under Section 31(7) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act must still operate within the statutory cap on post-award interest and cannot award a blanket, unexplained rate simply by invoking commercial reasonableness.

case: Konkan Bridge Corporation v. Eastern Rail Freight Ltd.
headline: A Sole-Arbitrator Clause Cannot Be Read as Requiring a Three-Member Tribunal Merely Because the Dispute Is Complex: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court set aside a High Court order that had, while appointing an arbitrator under Section 11, substituted a three-member tribunal for the sole-arbitrator mechanism the parties had actually agreed to, holding that a court's Section 11 power does not extend to rewriting the parties' own agreed composition of the tribunal, however complex the anticipated dispute.

case: Shree Industrial Fabricators v. Konkan Ferrous Ltd.
headline: Confidentiality Under Section 42A Does Not Bar a Party From Referring to Award Findings in a Related Court Proceeding: Bombay HC
summary: The Bombay High Court held that Section 42A's confidentiality obligation for arbitral proceedings does not prevent a party from referring to an arbitral award's findings in a separate, related court proceeding where doing so is reasonably necessary to protect or enforce the party's legal rights, distinguishing this from an unrestricted public disclosure of arbitration materials.

case: Union of India v. Gayatri Hydro Projects Ltd.
headline: A Section 34 Court Has No General Power to Modify an Arbitral Award — It Can Only Set Aside, Wholly or in Part: Supreme Court
summary: Resolving a long-running debate, a larger bench of the Supreme Court reaffirmed that a court exercising jurisdiction under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act does not have a general power to modify the substantive terms of an arbitral award, and is confined to either upholding the award or setting it aside, in whole or in severable part, on the recognised statutory grounds.

case: Precision Auto Components v. Karnataka MSE Facilitation Council
headline: An Award of the MSE Facilitation Council Under the MSMED Act Is Challenged Under Section 34 — Subject to the Act's Own 75% Pre-Deposit Condition: Karnataka HC
summary: The Karnataka High Court dismissed a buyer's Section 34 petition against an award rendered by the state's Micro and Small Enterprise Facilitation Council under Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006, for want of the mandatory seventy-five percent pre-deposit required under Section 19 of the MSMED Act, rejecting the buyer's argument that ordinary Section 34 procedure alone should govern the challenge.

case: Bhargava Township Developers v. Aditya Nirman Udyog
headline: An Arbitrator Who Earlier Acted as Conciliator in the Same Dispute Is Disqualified Absent the Parties' Express Written Consent: Delhi HC
summary: The Delhi High Court set aside the appointment of an arbitrator who had previously served as conciliator in the same dispute under a med-arb clause, holding that Section 80 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act bars a conciliator from acting as arbitrator in the same dispute unless the parties expressly agree otherwise in writing, and that this protection cannot be implied away merely because the med-arb clause its

case: Continental Retail Ventures v. Metro Junction Mall Pvt. Ltd.
headline: A Multi-Tier Dispute Resolution Clause Requiring Prior Negotiation Is Not a Jurisdictional Bar to Arbitration Once Invoked: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that a multi-tier dispute resolution clause requiring parties to first attempt good-faith negotiation before invoking arbitration is directory rather than a strict jurisdictional precondition, and that a party's failure to exhaust the negotiation step does not render a subsequently commenced arbitration itself without jurisdiction, particularly where the other party had shown no genuine willing

case: Vardhman Roadlines Pvt. Ltd. v. National Logistics Corporation
headline: A Section 21 Notice Invoking Arbitration Must Be Issued Within the Same Three-Year Limitation Period That Would Apply to a Civil Suit: Delhi HC
summary: The Delhi High Court held that the limitation period for issuing a notice invoking arbitration under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act runs from the date the cause of action accrues, and is governed by the same three-year period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 that would apply to a corresponding civil suit. A party cannot indefinitely defer invoking its arbitration clause once the under

case: In re: Mediated Settlement Agreement, Rohan Distributors v. Sunrise Apparel Exports
headline: A Mediated Settlement Agreement Under the Mediation Act, 2023 Is Enforceable as a Decree Without a Fresh Civil Suit: Delhi HC
summary: The Delhi High Court held that a mediated settlement agreement registered under Section 20 of the Mediation Act, 2023, whether reached through court-annexed or private mediation, can be enforced directly as if it were a decree of a civil court, without the settling party being put to the burden of filing a fresh civil suit to enforce the underlying settlement terms.

case: Novelty Prints Pvt. Ltd. v. Creative Canvas Studio
headline: A Copyright Licensing Dispute Is Arbitrable Even Though Copyright Itself Is a Right in Rem: Bombay HC
summary: The Bombay High Court held that a dispute over the terms of a copyright licence, as opposed to a challenge to the validity or subsistence of the copyright itself, is arbitrable, distinguishing between the underlying intellectual property right, which operates in rem and is not arbitrable, and a contractual licensing dispute between the specific parties, which operates in personam and can properly be resolved by arbit

case: Parsa Kente Collieries Ltd. v. Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Ltd.
headline: Supreme Court Replaces Retired Justice as Sole Arbitrator by Consent in Adani-Rajasthan DISCOM Dispute
summary: In a long-running power-sector arbitration between an Adani group company and a Rajasthan state DISCOM, the Supreme Court replaced retired Justice Arun Mishra as arbitrator, appointing Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul as sole arbitrator by consent of the parties. The order underscores the Court's continued willingness to step in and reconstitute a tribunal where the original arbitrator is unable to continue, keeping a long

case: M/S Steag Energy Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. GSPC Pipavav Power Company Ltd.
headline: Courts Must Exercise Restraint Reviewing Technical Tender & Contract-Award Decisions
summary: Ruling on an O&M contract dispute for a gas-based power plant, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's interference, holding that evaluation and award of complex technical contracts falls within the domain of the procuring authority and the competence of technical evaluators. Judicial interference is confined to cases of clear illegality, mala fides or irrationality.

case: Gujarat Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. Saryu Plastics Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Participation in Proceedings Without Objection Waives Challenge to Arbitrator's Mandate
summary: Justices Narasimha and Alok Aradhe upheld the validity of arbitral proceedings, holding that a party which participates in proceedings before an arbitral tribunal without raising a timely objection cannot subsequently challenge the arbitrator's mandate. The Court treated continued, unobjected participation as effective waiver of any procedural infirmity in the tribunal's constitution.

case: Home Care Retail Marts Pvt. Ltd. v. Haresh N. Sanghavi
headline: Section 9 Interim Relief Is Available Post-Award, Even to a Non-Award Holder
summary: Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan held that either party to an arbitration may seek interim measures under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act at any stage of the proceedings, including after the award is passed. The Court clarified that the expression "a party" in Section 9 draws no distinction between the successful and unsuccessful party, so even a non-award holder may seek interim protection.

case: NHAI v. Paras Ram — CMPMO Nos. 761–767 of 2025
headline: Holding Hearings at a Location Does Not Fix It as the Seat of Arbitration
summary: The Himachal Pradesh High Court, applying BALCO and BGS SGS SOMA, held that merely holding arbitration hearings at a location does not fix that place as the 'seat' of arbitration. Venue and seat are legally distinct. The first-filing rule under Section 42 locked in jurisdiction at the court having supervisory jurisdiction over the contractually specified seat — not the hearing venue.

case: Tamil Nadu Cements Corporation v. MSEFC — Writ Jurisdiction
headline: Writ Under Article 226 Maintainable Against MSEFC Where Order Is Passed Without Jurisdiction or Is a Nullity
summary: The Supreme Court held that a writ petition under Article 226 is maintainable against an order of the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFC) under Section 18 of the MSMED Act where the order is passed without jurisdiction, contrary to statutory procedure, or amounts to a nullity. While the MSMED Act provides a statutory remedy under Section 34/19, this does not bar exceptional writ jurisdiction.

case: IMAX Corp v. E-City Entertainment
headline: Non-Parties Impleaded at Enforcement Stage — Corporate Veil Pierced to Prevent Award Evasion
summary: The Bombay High Court held that where an affiliate or related entity benefited from a contract that is the subject of an arbitral award, non-parties to the arbitration may be impleaded at the enforcement and execution stage by piercing the corporate veil — preventing evasion of legal obligations through separate corporate structures.

case: Engineering Projects India v. MSA Global LLC Oman — CS(OS) 243/2025
headline: Rare Anti-Arbitration Injunction Granted Against Foreign Arbitration for Undisclosed Conflict
summary: The Delhi High Court granted an anti-arbitration injunction against ICC arbitration proceedings in Singapore, citing an arbitrator's undisclosed conflict of interest. The court invoked Section 34(2)(b)(ii) (public policy) and held that vexatious continuation of proceedings before a tribunal with an undisclosed conflict warrants intervention, even at a foreign seat, in extraordinary circumstances.

case: Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft Technologies — Hearing Commenced
headline: 5-Judge Constitution Bench Commences Hearing on Whether Courts Can Modify Arbitral Awards
summary: CJI Sanjiv Khanna led a five-judge Constitution Bench commencing detailed arguments on the foundational question: can Indian courts modify (not merely set aside) arbitral awards under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration Act? The bench identified two conflicting lines of authority — NHAI v. M. Hakeem (no modification) versus Vedanta/Tata Hydroelectric (modification permitted) — and reserved judgment after three deta

case: Jindal ITF Limited v. NTPC Limited
headline: Split Verdict Leaves Rs. 1,889 Crore Arbitral Award Against NTPC in Limbo, Referred to a Third Judge
summary: Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla delivered a split verdict on the validity of a roughly Rs. 1,889 crore award in favour of Jindal ITF against NTPC for wrongful termination of a coal-transportation agreement for the Farakka Thermal Power Plant — one Judge would have upheld the tribunal's findings, the other held the award could not be sustained. Referred to the Chief Justice for a third-judge or larger B

case: Arenel Private Limited v. M/s. Aakash Packaging
headline: An Award Relying on Irrelevant Material Over the Parties' Own Evidence Can Be Set Aside: Bombay High Court
summary: A Division Bench of the Bombay High Court held that an arbitral award that relies on irrelevant material or ignores relevant evidence on record violates fundamental principles of justice and can be set aside under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, upholding a Single Judge's decision that had set aside part of a December 2019 award in a packaging-materials supply dispute for reliance on hearsay

case: Spectrum Power Generation Limited v. GAIL (India) Limited
headline: An Arbitral Award Built on Inadmissible Evidence and Flawed Waiver/Estoppel Reasoning Is Set Aside: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court set aside an arbitral award that had rejected Spectrum Power Generation's claim for refund of GST reimbursed to GAIL (India) Limited on transmission charges under a Gas Sale Agreement, holding that the award was vitiated by patent illegality because it rested on inadmissible evidence and an erroneous application of the doctrines of waiver and estoppel.

case: Steel Authority of India Limited v. British Marine PLC
headline: Ruling on the Same Clause in an Earlier, Unrelated Arbitration Doesn't Disqualify an Arbitrator: Delhi High Court
summary: A Division Bench of Justices Prathiba M. Singh and Vikas Mahajan dismissed SAIL's challenge to an arbitral award in favour of British Marine, rejecting SAIL's argument that two tribunal members were disqualified merely because they had previously interpreted the same contractual clause (Clause 62) in a separate maritime arbitration involving SAIL. The Court held that such 'issue conflict' does not by itself give rise

case: Rajesh Kumar v. Union of India & Ors.
headline: Section 38 Has No Indigence Exception — Arbitral Fees Cannot Be Waived for Financial Incapacity
summary: After an arbitrator was appointed under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 through the Delhi International Arbitration Centre, the arbitral proceedings were terminated because the petitioner could not pay the DIAC's fees; the petitioner sought a judicial waiver or deferment of arbitral fees on grounds of financial incapacity, and a direction to frame a support mechanism for indigent claimants. case: Eco Green Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. v. Vikartan Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Admissions Made During Failed Conciliation Can't Decide the Arbitration, and an Arbitrator's 'Experience' Isn't Proof of Loss: Delhi HC
summary: In a Section 34 challenge arising from a Greater Noida construction project dispute, Justice Avneesh Jhingan set aside an arbitral award (and additional award) after finding the tribunal had relied on admissions made during a failed conciliation to decide the arbitration, holding that conciliation proceedings remain confidential even once settlement talks fail. The Court also held that an arbitrator's personal experi

case: Star Pipe Products India Pvt. Ltd. v. Ashirwad Foundries Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Commercial Division Directs Sale of Mortgaged Property in Execution of a Money Decree
summary: Justice Aniruddha Roy, sitting in the Commercial Division of the Calcutta High Court, directed the sale of mortgaged property to satisfy a decree obtained by the decree-holder, underscoring the Division's continuing role in enforcing commercial money decrees efficiently once liability has been finally adjudicated.

case: High Point Supply Company LLC v. Agati Healthcare Private Limited
headline: Seeking Monetary Relief Alongside Urgent Interim Relief Does Not Defeat the Section 12-A Mediation Exception
summary: Justices R.I. Chagla and Farhan P. Dubash restored a US distributor's commercial suit rejected for want of pre-institution mediation, clarifying that whether a suit "contemplates urgent interim relief" — the exception to mandatory Section 12-A mediation — calls for only a limited jurisdictional inquiry, not an assessment of merits or likelihood of the relief actually being granted.

case: Ram Lakhan Shukla v. Hintek Electronics Private Limited & Anr.
headline: Salary and Increment Disputes Are Not 'Commercial Disputes' — Return the Plaint, Don't Dismiss the Suit: Delhi HC
summary: Justices Prathiba M. Singh and Vikas Mahajan held that disputes arising from an employment contract — including claims for salary arrears and increments — do not qualify as a 'commercial dispute' under Section 2(c) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. The Bench upheld the finding that the underlying dispute between the employee and Hintek Electronics was not commercial in nature, but modified the order below to direct

case: Vertex Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. Riverside Traders
headline: Interim Injunction Restraining Breach of a Negative Covenant Granted Without Requiring Proof of Quantifiable Loss
summary: The Delhi High Court granted an interim injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC restraining a distributor from selling a competing product line in breach of an exclusivity covenant in its distribution agreement, holding that breach of a clear negative covenant in a commercial contract itself supports a finding of irreparable injury, since the harm to a manufacturer's distribution strategy is not easily reduced

case: Ashford Leasing Ltd. v. Greenfield Industries Pvt. Ltd.
headline: An Indemnity Clause Is Not a Guarantee — Liability Under Each Arises Differently and Cannot Be Conflated
summary: The Bombay High Court, in a commercial dispute over a supply agreement, clarified the settled but frequently blurred distinction between an indemnity clause and a guarantee, holding that an indemnity creates a primary, independent obligation to make good a specified loss, whereas a guarantee creates a secondary obligation contingent on the principal debtor's default, and that a clause drafted loosely using both terms

case: Highgate Pharma Pvt. Ltd. v. Continental Packaging Co.
headline: A Party Cannot Withhold Relevant Documents in a Commercial Suit by Selectively Disclosing Only Favourable Correspondence
summary: In a commercial suit governed by the disclosure obligations under the Commercial Courts Act, the Delhi High Court directed a defendant to produce its complete email correspondence with the plaintiff, holding that selective disclosure of only favourable communications while withholding the rest defeats the purpose of the Act's document-disclosure regime and can attract adverse costs consequences.

case: Zenith Constructions Ltd. v. Falcon Engineering Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Expert Evidence on Technical Valuation Cannot Substitute the Court's Own Assessment of Contractual Liability
summary: The Karnataka High Court, while admitting expert evidence on the technical valuation of construction work in a commercial dispute over defective execution, clarified that an expert's opinion assists the court on technical questions but cannot substitute the court's own determination of contractual liability and breach, which remains a legal question for the court to decide on the totality of evidence.

case: Coastal Hardware Dealers' Collective v. Union Fasteners Ltd.
headline: A Representative Suit Under Order I Rule 8 CPC Permitted for a Common Grievance Shared by a Class of Dealers
summary: The Madras High Court permitted a representative suit under Order I Rule 8 CPC to proceed on behalf of a class of dealers with a common grievance against a supplier's unilateral change to credit terms, holding that where numerous dealers share an identical interest and cause of action, a representative suit avoids a multiplicity of individual proceedings and is an appropriate procedural route even in a purely commerc

case: Meritage Traders Pvt. Ltd. v. Sunrise Wholesalers
headline: A Running Account Between Commercial Parties Extends Limitation for Each Fresh Acknowledgment of Balance
summary: The Delhi High Court held that in a recovery suit for unpaid commercial dues arising out of a running account between a supplier and a buyer, each signed acknowledgment of the outstanding balance, including in periodic account reconciliation statements, constitutes a fresh acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, extending the limitation period from the date of each such acknowledgment.

case: Windsor Apparel Exports v. Nortex Fabrics Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Limitation for a Commercial Suit Runs From the Date of Breach, Not From When the Loss Was Fully Quantified
summary: The Gujarat High Court held that the three-year limitation period under Article 1 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for a suit on a running account, and the equivalent period for a suit founded on breach of contract, runs from the date the breach occurred or the cause of action arose, and not from the later date on which the claimant was able to fully quantify its loss, rejecting an argument that limitation should be recko

case: Amberline Traders v. Northgate Distributors
headline: Rejection of Goods for Breach of Condition Under the Sale of Goods Act Requires Timely Notice, Not Just a Defect
summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court, in a commercial dispute over a bulk consignment of goods rejected for quality non-conformity, held that a buyer's right to reject goods for breach of a condition under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 is lost if not exercised within a reasonable time after delivery; a genuine defect in the goods is not, by itself, enough if the buyer's rejection notice comes too late and the buyer is fou

case: Continental Fastening Systems v. Apex B2B Marketplace Pvt. Ltd.
headline: An Unreasonably Restrictive Exclusivity Clause Imposed on a Smaller Commercial Counterparty Can Be Struck Down as an Unfair Trade Practice
summary: The Delhi High Court struck down an exclusivity clause imposed by a dominant platform operator on a smaller B2B seller, holding that where a stronger commercial party leverages unequal bargaining power to impose an unreasonably one-sided restrictive covenant with no corresponding benefit to the weaker party, the clause can be treated as an unfair trade practice and refused enforcement, even outside the strict confine

case: M. Gagan Bothra v. Senthil Kumar
headline: Foreign Residence Is No Bar to a Section 95 IBC Petition Against a Personal Guarantor: NCLT Chennai
summary: Admitting a Section 95 IBC application against a personal guarantor who resisted the petition partly on the ground that he resided abroad, the NCLT Chennai Bench held the Code does not restrict its applicability to personal guarantors based on nationality or place of residence, particularly where the guarantee was executed with a Chennai address and the underlying corporate debtor was based in Chennai.

case: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth v. Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.
headline: A Section 94 Personal Insolvency Plea Cannot Be Used to Stall SARFAESI Recovery: NCLAT
summary: Dismissing a personal guarantor's appeal, NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that his Section 94 IBC application was really an attempt to obtain an interim moratorium and obstruct the bank's lawful recovery and SARFAESI enforcement rather than a genuine bid at insolvency resolution, holding that such applications must be pursued in good faith for actual resolution, not as a shield against creditor enforcement.

case: Bhumika Nilay R. Shah & Ors. v. Prawincharan Prafulcharan Dwary & Ors.
headline: Personal Guarantors Cannot Reopen a Final DRT Liability Finding Through Section 114 IBC Proceedings: NCLAT
summary: Dismissing appeals by three personal guarantors of Archon Engicon Ltd., NCLAT held that because the Debt Recovery Tribunal's 2021 order upholding the guarantee and fixing joint and several liability for over Rs. 149.26 crore had attained finality and was never challenged, the guarantors could not re-agitate the extent of that liability in collateral proceedings under Section 114 of the IBC.

case: Duke Fashions (India) Ltd. & Anr. v. Pramod Kumar Misra (Liquidator of Venus Garments (India) Ltd.) & Ors.
headline: A Liquidator Can Recover Possession Through the NCLT Without Going to a Rent Controller: NCLAT
summary: Dismissing occupants' appeals against an NCLT eviction order, NCLAT held that a liquidator's recovery of a corporate debtor's premises does not convert the dispute into a landlord-tenant matter, so occupants cannot invoke state rent-control legislation, such as the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, to resist a liquidator's possession claim before the NCLT.

case: Jones Lang LaSalle Property Consultants (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. M. A. Leasing and Construction Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
headline: Time Spent Pursuing a Failed Section 9 IBC Petition Can Be Excluded When Computing Limitation for a Follow-On Suit
summary: The Calcutta High Court (Commercial Division) admitted a money suit filed after the plaintiff's earlier Section 9 IBC petition was dismissed by the NCLT on the ground of a pre-existing dispute. Applying Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act, the Court held that a dismissal at the threshold for pre-existing dispute — without any adjudication on merits — qualifies as a "defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nat

case: IBBI v. Truvisory Insolvency Professionals — Feb 27, 2026
headline: Section 198 IBC Cannot Be Used to Condone Delay in NCLAT Appeals Beyond Section 61(2) Limit
summary: The NCLAT held that Section 198 IBC, which empowers condonation of delays in performance of statutory functions by IBBI, cannot be invoked to condone delay in filing appeals before the NCLAT beyond the outer limit prescribed in Section 61(2). The IBBI's 103-day delay was held un-condonable. Section 198 is limited to adjudicating authority proceedings — not appellate proceedings before NCLAT.

case: Catalyst Trusteeship v. Ecstasy Realty Pvt. Ltd.
headline: SC Restores ₹600 Crore Insolvency Plea — NCLT/NCLAT Findings Called Perverse and Unsustainable
summary: The Supreme Court set aside concurrent NCLT and NCLAT rulings rejecting Catalyst Trusteeship's Section 7 petition as perverse — based on surmises, conjectures, and assumptions. The Court held that informal restructuring negotiations cannot override the binding terms of a Debenture Trust Deed. The ₹600 crore CIRP was restored and initiation of CIRP directed.

case: Kalyani Transco v. BPSL — Recall Order
headline: Supreme Court Recalls Liquidation Order — CoC Is Not Functus Officio After Plan Approval
summary: In a significant follow-up order, the Supreme Court recalled its earlier liquidation order in the BPSL case after further review. The Court held that the Committee of Creditors does not become functus officio once a resolution plan is approved — it continues to function until full plan implementation. The Court also clarified the scope of Section 32A IBC protection against ED/PMLA attachments.

case: Aayush Prashant Agarwal v. Uma Export Limited & Klass Insolvency Resolution Professionals Private Limited
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
headline: NCLAT Allows CIRP Withdrawal After Settlement Under the Tightened 2026 Section 12A Regime
summary: The NCLAT Principal Bench permitted the Interim Resolution Professional of Epic Yarns Private Limited to move the NCLT for withdrawal of an admitted CIRP under Section 12A of the IBC, following a post-admission settlement between operational creditor Uma Export Limited and the corporate debtor, applying the withdrawal framework as substituted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2026.

case: Tata Capital Financial Services Limited v. Neel Motors LLP & Ors.
headline: The 2026 Amendment Excluding Personal Guarantors From the IBC Moratorium Applies to Cases Already Pending: Bombay High Court
summary: Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan held that the amendment inserting Section 96(4) of the IBC, effective 26 May 2026, which excludes personal guarantors of corporate debtors from the interim moratorium under Section 96, applies to Section 95 applications that were already pending as of that date. The Court reasoned that the statutory phrase 'where an application is filed' covers anything filed and still pending on the eff

case: Bank of Baroda v. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Ors. (In the matter of Reliance Communications Infrastructure Ltd.)
headline: A CoC Cannot Rework an Approved Resolution Plan's Distribution Formula After the Fact
summary: After the resolution plan for Reliance Communications Infrastructure Ltd. was approved, the Committee of Creditors, at a meeting held on 27 October 2023, passed a resolution by 67.55% majority to reassign and reallocate proceeds of the 'Reliance Bhutan Loan' in favour of financial creditors who had dissented from the plan; IDBI Bank and SBI objected. The NCLT held the CoC had no power to alter the plan's distribution

case: Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd. v. Neel Motors LLP & Ors.
headline: IBC Section 96(4)'s Guarantor-Moratorium Exclusion Applies Retroactively to Pending Cases
summary: After Neel Motors LLP went into liquidation, Tata Capital sought to proceed with arbitration against the individual personal guarantors, who argued that pending Section 95 insolvency applications against them triggered an interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC. case: Mukesh Goyal v. CA Santanu Brahma & Anr. (In re: Aanchal Ispat Ltd.)
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Kolkata Bench
headline: A Pending Appellate Challenge Can Shift a Resolution Plan's Implementation Clock Even Without a Formal Stay: NCLT Kolkata
summary: In a dispute over when implementation timelines under an approved resolution plan for Aanchal Ispat Ltd. began to run, the applicant sought a direction that the 'NCLT Approval Date' for commencement and implementation under Clause (oo) of the plan be treated as 11.08.2025, the date the successful resolution applicant's own appeal (limited to observations in the approval order) was filed. case: S. Viswanathan v. Canara Bank
headline: CoC's Decision to Replace a Resolution Professional Is Protected by Commercial Wisdom: NCLAT Chennai
summary: A Bench of Justice N. Seshasayee and Jatindranath Swain upheld the Committee of Creditors' decision to replace a resolution professional, holding that such a replacement falls within the CoC's commercial wisdom, provided the statutory route is followed, and that the Tribunal cannot interfere with it — while leaving the replaced RP's claim for professional fees and CIRP expenses open for adjudication by the NCLT.

case: State Bank of India v. Maithan Alloys Limited & Ors.
headline: A Concluded Liquidation Auction Cannot Be Reopened for a Later, Higher Offer Alone: NCLAT
summary: The NCLAT set aside an Adjudicating Authority order that had interfered with a concluded liquidation e-auction, holding that the auction had not been challenged for fraud, collusion or irregularity, and that the sanctity of a public auction in liquidation cannot be disturbed merely because a subsequent higher offer was later made.

case: ASR Market Ventures Private Limited v. Fitship Private Limited & Anr.
headline: Occasional Use Alongside a House Mark Does Not Create Standalone Trademark Rights: Delhi High Court
summary: Dismissing FITPASS owner ASR Market Ventures' rectification petition against Fitship's registered FITFEAST mark and refusing an interim injunction, Justice Jyoti Singh held ASR's own records showed it had consistently promoted its business under the umbrella mark FITPASS, with only scant, non-source-identifying references to FITFEAST, so it failed to establish independent goodwill in that term.

case: Graviss Foods Private Limited v. Registrar of Trade Marks
headline: 'ICE CREAM ROCKS' Is Too Generic and Descriptive to Register as a Trademark: Bombay High Court
summary: Dismissing Baskin Robbins licensee Graviss Foods' challenge to the Registrar's refusal to register 'ICE CREAM ROCKS', Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan held the phrase lacked the distinctive character needed for registration under Sections 9(1)(a) and 9(1)(b) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, being too generic and descriptive of the goods despite the brand's marketing use.

case: Hermès International v. Macky Lifestyle
headline: Delhi High Court Declares the Birkin Bag Shape and HERMES Marks Well Known, Decrees Permanent Injunction
summary: The Delhi High Court held that the Birkin bag's three-dimensional shape and the HERMES word and device marks have acquired extensive recognition and association with the plaintiff, declaring them well known under the Trade Marks Act and decreeing a permanent injunction against the defendant's sale of lookalike products.

case: DS Intellectual Properties LLP & Anr. v. Abhinav Singh & Ors.
headline: Delhi High Court Declares the DS Group Name and Logo Well-Known Trademarks, Grants Permanent Injunction
summary: The Delhi High Court declared the "DS Group" name and its corresponding logo to be well-known trademarks under Section 2(1)(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and granted a permanent injunction restraining a defendant's operation of a website impersonating an authorised dealership of the group's products.

case: Jain Shikanji Pvt. Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Jain
headline: Delhi HC Refuses to Accept an Unconditional Apology, Upholds Contempt Finding Over Continued Use of an Injuncted Mark
summary: Justice Jyoti Singh upheld a trial court's refusal to accept an unconditional apology tendered by a company director found guilty, under Order XXXIX Rule 2A CPC, of wilfully violating an injunction restraining use of the "Jain Shikanji" trademark, affirming arrest warrants and property attachment while reducing the exemplary costs imposed from ₹5 lakh to ₹3 lakh.

case: Parle Products Pvt. Ltd. v. Registrar of Trade Marks & Anr.
headline: Earlier Trademark Filing Date Prevails Over Later, More Extensive Commercial Use
summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed Parle's appeal against registration of the "20-20" mark for biscuits in favour of a rival applicant who had filed on a "proposed to be used" basis one week before Parle began using the mark commercially, holding under Section 18 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 that filing seniority — not the extent of subsequent market use — determines who is the true proprietor where both parties filed on

case: ADS Spirits v. Registrar of Trade Marks
headline: 'Uniqueness' Is Not the Test for Trademark Registration — Distinctiveness Under Section 9(1)(a) Suffices
summary: The Delhi High Court held that a mark need not be wholly unique to qualify for registration under Section 9(1)(a) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — distinctiveness in relation to the goods or services concerned is the governing standard. The Court also directed the Trade Marks Registry to pass reasoned, speaking orders when refusing applications rather than terse rejections.

case: InterDigital Patent Holdings Inc. v. Shenzhen Transsion Holdings Co. Ltd.
headline: Delhi HC Clarifies Power to Direct Pro Tem Security in SEP & FRAND Disputes
summary: The Court held that it may direct an implementer to deposit pro tem security in a complex Standard Essential Patent infringement suit even before a detailed examination of the merits, balancing the interests of SEP holders against those of implementers. The ruling is a significant contribution to India's developing FRAND jurisprudence in the telecommunications sector.

case: Novartis AG & Anr. v. Venkata Narayana Active Ingredients Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Bolar Exception Is Narrowly Construed — Burden Is on the Party Invoking Section 107A
summary: The Madras High Court held that the Bolar exception under Section 107A of the Patents Act is a narrowly construed statutory carve-out intended exclusively to facilitate regulatory approvals, not a general exemption for research or commercial exports. The evidentiary burden rests on the party invoking the exception to demonstrate a genuine regulatory purpose behind the impugned activity.

case: CCI v. Ericsson — Standard Essential Patents and Competition Law
headline: Landmark Policy Moment: SC Ruling to Define Whether FRAND Disputes Go to Patent Courts or CCI
summary: The Supreme Court's consideration of the CCI v. Ericsson matter on standard essential patents (SEPs) is expected to definitively clarify whether FRAND licensing disputes are governed by patent law or competition law in India — determining whether the CCI has jurisdiction to investigate SEP licensing violations as anti-competitive conduct. This is of enormous commercial significance for telecoms, IoT, and automotive s

case: 7-Eleven Inc. v. Trademark Registry — 'Big Bite' Mark Rejected
headline: International Reputation Alone Cannot Establish Protectable Goodwill in India
summary: The Madras High Court upheld the rejection of 7-Eleven's 'Big Bite' trademark application, ruling that a company's international reputation does not automatically translate into protectable goodwill in India for passing-off purposes. Actual business presence and consumer recognition in India must be independently established.

case: Sumitomo Rubber Industries v. Dunlop International — TEMPAPO-IPD 5/2025
headline: Unreasoned Trademark Registrar Orders Set Aside — IP Division Demands Fully Reasoned Decisions
summary: Calcutta's newly established IP Division set aside unreasoned Deputy Registrar of Trademarks orders that had allowed registration of the 'Dunlop' word mark for eight product categories. The IP Division stressed the critical importance of procedural fairness, detailed consideration of all material facts (including fraud allegations), and the necessity of comprehensive reasoned decisions in trademark adjudication.

case: Amazon Technologies v. Lifestyle Equities CV — E-Commerce Platform Liability
headline: E-Commerce Platforms Face Trademark Liability for Hosting Infringing Third-Party Listings
summary: The Delhi High Court examined Amazon's intermediary defences against the Beverly Hills Polo Club (BHPC) trademark owner's claims for counterfeit listings. The Court scrutinised the adequacy of notice-and-takedown mechanisms, setting important standards for the proactive obligations of online marketplaces in removing infringing product listings after being put on notice.

case: Pidilite v. Sanjay Jain — 'KWIKHEAL' Mark
headline: Monopoly Over Common/Descriptive Terms in Trademarks Cannot Be Claimed
summary: The Delhi High Court refused Pidilite's application to cancel the 'KWIKHEAL' trademark, holding that Pidilite could not claim monopoly over the term 'Kwik' or its variations as a generic or descriptive element common to the adhesive trade. The ruling clarified that exclusivity cannot extend to generic elements of a brand that are common to the trade.

case: Royal Challengers Sports v. Uber India Systems — RCB Trademark
headline: Sports Franchise Trademark Rights Examined Against Commercial Partnership Usage
summary: The Delhi High Court examined the scope of trademark protection available to the Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) IPL franchise in a dispute with Uber India over alleged unauthorised use of RCB branding in a promotional campaign, setting important parameters for brand licensing rights in Indian sport and the intersection of trademark law with commercial partnerships.

case: Johnson & Johnson v. Pritamdas Arora — IP Division
headline: ₹3.34 Crore Damages Awarded for Counterfeit Medical Devices — Public Health Aggravation
summary: The Delhi High Court awarded ₹3.34 crore (approx. US$400,800) to Johnson & Johnson against a manufacturer of counterfeit medical devices. The Court emphasised that counterfeiting of medical devices that could physically harm patients is treated with particular severity — aggravated damages are available in pharmaceutical and medical device IP infringement cases.

case: Conqueror Innovations Private Limited & Anr. v. Xiaomi Technology India Private Limited
headline: A Nine-Year Delay in Seeking an Interim Injunction Is, By Itself, Sufficient to Deny Relief: Delhi High Court
summary: Justices V. Kameswar Rao and Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora upheld refusal to injunct Xiaomi's 'Find Device' anti-theft feature, holding Xiaomi's system did not prima facie contain the essential features of the appellant's patented device-finder system, and that the appellant's roughly nine-year delay in seeking interim relief was independently fatal, particularly as the patent was due to expire shortly after the hearing

case: Hindustan Unilever Limited v. Kwick Living (I) Private Limited
headline: Where Can You Sue Over Online Trademark Infringement? Delhi High Court Refers the Question to a Larger Bench
summary: In HUL's disparagement and trademark suit over Kwick Living's comparative advertising campaign against Vim and Surf Excel, a Division Bench (Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani) held that principles of territorial jurisdiction are not diluted merely because allegedly infringing content is accessible over the internet across India. While deciding jurisdiction for the dispute before it, the Bench referred to a Larger Bench t

case: Havells India Limited & Anr. v. Havai Home Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
headline: Your Own Trademark Registration Is No Defence to a Passing-Off Claim Over a Deceptively Similar Mark: Delhi High Court
summary: Justice Jyoti Singh held that a defendant's own trademark registration for 'HAVAI' is no defence to a passing-off action where the plaintiff shows prior goodwill in 'HAVELLS', deceptive similarity and likelihood of consumer confusion, and restrained Havai Home Products from using the 'HAVAI' word and device marks, or any other mark deceptively similar to the Havells marks, assessing passing off by reference to actual

case: Rajat Sharma & Independent News Service Pvt. Ltd. v. Tamara Doc & Ors.
headline: Delhi High Court Permanently Restrains AI Deepfakes Misusing a Journalist's Persona and Voice
summary: Justice Jyoti Singh granted a decree of permanent injunction in favour of India TV chairman Rajat Sharma and Independent News Service Pvt. Ltd. against several Facebook pages and two YouTube channels that had used AI-generated deepfake videos carrying distorted, modulated versions of Sharma's image and voice, restraining further infringement of his personality and publicity rights and misuse of India TV's registered

case: Rukhmani Keshwani (trading as Vishwas Agarbatti Store) v. Raju Agarbatti Works & Anr.
headline: An Online Marketplace Listing Reachable in a City Is Enough to Confer Territorial Jurisdiction There: Delhi High Court
summary: A Division Bench of the Delhi High Court restored a trademark and copyright infringement suit over the 'RADHEY KRISHNA' agarbatti mark between two Rajasthan-based manufacturers, holding that a trial court had wrongly returned the plaint for want of territorial jurisdiction. The Court found that listings for the defendant's goods accessible and purchasable in Delhi via the IndiaMart online marketplace were sufficient

case: JCB India Ltd. v. Anonymous Persons/Entities & Anr. (arising from dispute with Krishna Auto Riders Pvt. Ltd.)
headline: Ex Parte Injunction and Google/Meta Takedown Granted Against Anonymous Accounts Misusing JCB's Marks
summary: After JCB India's dealership dispute with Krishna Auto Riders Pvt. Ltd. (KARPL) was referred to arbitration, anonymous online accounts allegedly linked to KARPL began using JCB's name, logos and other brand identifiers, and circulated videos and Instagram reels falsely claiming two JCB India officers had been arrested. Justice Jyoti Singh found JCB had established a prima facie case and that the balance of convenienc

case: Rukhmani Keshwani (Trading as Vishwas Agarbatti Store) v. Raju Agarbatti Works & Anr.
headline: Online Marketplace Listings Reachable From a Forum Can Found Territorial Jurisdiction
summary: The plaintiff, claiming prior use since 1995 of the 'RADHEY KRISHNA' trademark and trade dress for agarbattis, had her infringement suit returned by a Trial Court for want of territorial jurisdiction since both parties operated from Rajasthan. A Division Bench of Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla restored the suit, holding that the Rajasthan-based defendants' IndiaMart listings (complete with GST details

case: Herbalife International, Inc. v. Ashish Kumar & Ors.
headline: Delhi HC Restrains 'Herbawish' as Deceptively Similar to Herbalife's Marks and Trade Dress
summary: In a trademark infringement suit by Herbalife International over its 'HERBALIFE'/'HERBALIFE NUTRITION' word marks, three-leaf device logo and product marks including 'Formula 1', 'Afresh' and 'Cell-U-Loss', Justice Jyoti Singh temporarily restrained the defendants from using 'Herbawish', 'Herbawish Nutrition', a similar three-leaf logo, and similar trade dress for nutritional products. The Court found a strong prima

case: Nova Chemtech Ltd. v. Opposition Board (Patent Office)
headline: Post-Grant Opposition Must Be Decided Within the Statutory Framework of Section 25(2), Delay Alone Is No Ground to Bypass It
summary: Reviewing a challenge to prolonged post-grant opposition proceedings, the tribunal held that the structured process under Section 25(2) of the Patents Act (reference to an Opposition Board, a reasoned recommendation, and a hearing before the Controller) must be followed even where proceedings have taken longer than the indicative timelines suggest, though it directed the Controller to expedite the pending recommendat

case: Innoview Analytics Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajat Malhotra
headline: Court Enforces Post-Employment Confidentiality Obligation Over Proprietary Client Algorithms, Absent Any Trade Secrets Statute
summary: In the absence of a dedicated trade secrets statute, the Court granted an injunction restraining a former employee from using or disclosing proprietary analytics methodologies, applying the equitable doctrine of breach of confidence read together with an express confidentiality clause in the employment contract, and finding the information had the necessary quality of confidence.

case: Vantage Lifestyle Brands Pvt. Ltd. v. Unknown Persons/Entities
headline: Court Grants a John Doe / Ashok Kumar Order Ahead of a Festive-Season Counterfeiting Surge
summary: Anticipating a seasonal spike in counterfeit sales of its branded goods, a consumer lifestyle company obtained an ex parte injunction against unnamed and unidentified infringers, authorising a Local Commissioner to conduct search-and-seizure raids at markets known for counterfeit sales and directing online marketplaces to take down flagged listings.

case: Zenith Materials Technologies Ltd. v. Prakash Industrial Coatings Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Royalty Clause in a Technology Transfer Agreement Interpreted Against the Licensor for Ambiguity
summary: In a dispute over a technology licensing and transfer agreement for a proprietary industrial coating process, the Court held that an ambiguous royalty computation clause must be interpreted against the party that drafted it, awarding the licensee a lower royalty base than the licensor claimed, and stressed the importance of precisely defined royalty triggers in technology transfer agreements.

case: Codeforge Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Aditya Ranjan Pillai
headline: Court Grants Interim Relief Over Unauthorised Reproduction of Proprietary Source Code, Applying Copyright to Software
summary: Recognising that computer programs are protected as 'literary works' under Section 2(o) of the Copyright Act, 1957, the Court granted an interim injunction restraining a former contractor from using or distributing source code substantially derived from the claimant's proprietary software, following a code-comparison analysis showing extensive structural similarity.

case: Radiant Consumer Brands Ltd. v. Kavya Distributors Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Court Distinguishes an IP Assignment From a Licence Where a Distribution Agreement's Wording Was Ambiguous
summary: In a dispute over whether a distribution agreement effected a permanent assignment of trademark rights or merely a licence to use the mark during the distribution term, the Court held that in the absence of clear assignment language and registry recordation, the arrangement must be construed as a licence, which terminated on expiry of the distribution agreement.

case: Impresario Entertainment and Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. v. The Shake Social (trading as Social Circle)
headline: Delhi HC Grants Interim Injunction Against 'Social Circle', Building On Its Earlier Well-Known-Mark Finding for 'SOCIAL'
summary: Building on its January 2026 declaration of 'SOCIAL' as a well-known trademark in a related suit, Justice Vikas Mahajan granted an interim injunction restraining a Dehradun restaurant trading as 'Social Circle' from using a mark deceptively similar to Impresario's 'SOCIAL' brand for restaurant and bar services.

case: M.K. Suresh Kumar v. Union of India — Challenge to the Four Labour Codes
headline: Kerala HC Delivers First Reported High Court Ruling on the Four Labour Codes' Validity
summary: In the first reported High Court judgment testing the constitutionality of the Labour Codes since their November 2025 implementation, the Kerala High Court applied the manifest-arbitrariness test from Shayara Bano v. Union of India in upholding aspects of the Codes' rule-making and inspection framework, while leaving the door open for further Supreme Court examination of the right-to-strike and inspection regime.

case: Vaneeta Patnaik v. Nirmal Kanti Chakrabarti & Ors.
headline: Delayed POSH Complaints Are Time-Barred and Cannot Be Examined on Merits
summary: The Supreme Court addressed the limitation period for filing complaints under the POSH Act, holding that a complaint filed well beyond the prescribed period was time-barred and could not be examined on merits — while directing, as a separate matter, that the judgment itself form a permanent part of the respondent's résumé.

case: Vinod Kumar & Ors. v. Union of India
headline: Temporary Employees in Continuous Service for 25+ Years Must Be Regularised
summary: The Supreme Court directed regularisation of temporary accounts clerks who had worked for over 25 years on the same duties as permanent employees, noting the similarity in selection, duties, and promotion procedures. Back wages were also directed to be paid.

case: Union of India v. Ex. Lt. Selina John
headline: Dismissal of Female Employee for Marital Status Is Unconstitutional Gender Discrimination
summary: The Supreme Court reaffirmed that dismissing a female employee based solely on her marital status constitutes unconstitutional gender discrimination, violating the fundamental right to equality under Article 14. Service rules and contracts that impose differential marital-status conditions exclusively on female employees are invalid.

case: Mahanadi Coalfields v. Brajrajnagar Coal Mines Workers' Union
headline: Contract Workers Performing Permanent/Perennial Work Must Be Regularised
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that workers assigned to tasks of a permanent or ongoing nature cannot lawfully be classified as contract workers under the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970. Denial of regularisation to workers performing the same duties as regular employees — especially under an existing settlement — amounts to wrongful denial of employment.

case: X v. Internal Complaints Committee & Ors.
headline: POSH Act Applicable to Gig Workers — Platform Aggregators Must Ensure Safe Environment
summary: The Karnataka High Court upheld the applicability of the Prevention of Sexual Harassment (POSH) Act, 2013, to gig workers, and emphasised the obligation of platform aggregators to ensure a safe working environment for such workers. A final ruling is awaited and is expected to be landmark in gig economy labour rights.

case: Rakesh Kumar Verma v. HDFC Bank / HDFC Bank v. Deepti Bhatia
headline: Exclusive Jurisdiction Clauses in Employment Contracts Are Valid and Enforceable
summary: The Supreme Court upheld exclusive jurisdiction clauses in private employment contracts, holding that parties may contractually agree to confer exclusive jurisdiction on a specific court for employment-related disputes, provided that court has inherent territorial jurisdiction under Section 20 CPC and the clause clearly and expressly excludes all other courts.

case: Vijaya Bank v. Prashant B. Narnaware
headline: Employment Bonds and Minimum Service Clauses Are Valid Liquidated Damage Provisions
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of an indemnity bond requiring payment of ₹2 lakh upon resignation before completing three years, holding that restrictive covenants operative during the employment term (as opposed to post-employment restraints) do not constitute restraint of trade under Section 27 of the Contract Act. The objective is to protect the employer's recruitment and training investment.

case: Prabhat Kumar Singh & Ors. v. Accu Pack Engineering Pvt. Ltd.
headline: Employers Can Only Forfeit Gratuity to the Extent of Actually Proven Loss, Not Bare Allegations: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that under Section 4(6) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employer's right to forfeit gratuity of an employee terminated for misconduct causing loss is limited strictly to the loss actually proved, rejecting the employer's claim of a Rs. 50 lakh loss for lack of independent evidence such as an audit report. case: Union of India & Ors. v. Sh. Jamuna Dass
headline: Gratuity Can Be Withheld Through the Entire Pendency of a Criminal Appeal
summary: A former Tax Assistant in the Income Tax Department, who superannuated on 31 December 2011 and was convicted by a Special Judge on 23 January 2012, argued his gratuity claim should not remain frozen while his criminal appeal against that conviction stayed pending before the High Court. case: Hari Prakash v. New Delhi Municipal Council
headline: A Bare Assertion of 'Abandonment of Service' Cannot Defeat an Illegal-Termination Finding Without Supporting Records
summary: NDMC challenged a Labour Court award holding a workman's services illegally terminated, arguing the workman had voluntarily abandoned service. case: FSS Act Overriding Effect — Ram Nath v. State of UP Applied
headline: FSSA Overrides IPC — Simultaneous Food Adulteration Prosecution Under IPC Barred
summary: Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Ram Nath v. State of UP [(2024) 3 SCC 502] that the FSSA has overriding effect over all other laws including the IPC under Section 89, multiple courts applied this principle in 2025 to quash parallel IPC food adulteration prosecutions. Charges under IPC Sections 272 and 273 cannot run alongside FSSA Section 59 proceedings.

case: ITC Limited v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Ors.
headline: Delhi High Court Restrains FSSAI From Cancelling ITC's Licence Over '100% Atta' Labelling Claims, Pending Hearing
summary: Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma granted interim protection to ITC Limited, restraining FSSAI from cancelling its food business licence over advisories objecting to the '100% Atta', '100% Madhya Pradesh Wheat' and '0% Maida' claims on Aashirvaad MP Chakki Atta packaging, pending further hearing listed for 9 September 2026. summary: A Food Inspector had seized coriander powder from a train pantry car in 2004 on suspicion of adulteration; the accused were prosecuted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 but were never informed of their statutory right under Section 13(2) of the Act to have the counterpart sample independently analysed by the Central Food Laboratory. case: M/s Singla Traders v. State of Haryana & Ors.
headline: A Food Safety Officer Has No Power to Seize Plant and Machinery

case: Siddharth Agro v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.

case: P.B. Agro LLP v. Union of India & Ors.
headline: A Writ Against an FDA Show-Cause Notice Belongs in the State Where It Was Issued, Not Wherever Is Convenient: Delhi HC
summary: P.B. Agro LLP, master licensee for the 'VIMAL' brand of elaichi and pan masala (not containing tobacco), sought to quash a show cause notice issued by Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration to its brand ambassadors and to restrain coercive action over alleged non-compliance with food safety norms. case: Shivam Traders and Hire Purchase Pvt. Ltd. v. Madhusudan Vehicles Pvt. Ltd.

summary: Dismissing a borrower's appeal seeking an injunction against an NBFC's premature recovery of a nine-year loan facility, the Allahabad High Court held that under Section 45QA of the RBI Act, 1934 read with Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, only the NCLT has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning premature repayment of a deposit or loan from an NBFC, and a civil court cannot grant an injunction restraining such r

case: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat v. Punjab National Bank & Ors.

summary: Refusing to direct PNB to accept a Rs. 22.50 crore one-time settlement proposed by the legal heirs of a personal guarantor after three group companies were ordered into liquidation, the NCLT Guwahati Bench held that accepting an OTS proposal is a matter of commercial discretion for the lender, and the Tribunal has no power to compel a financial creditor to accept a settlement that was never crystallised into a bindin

case: Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
headline: Repossession Power Must Be Exercised With 'Great Circumspection' — Cannot Become a Licence to Seize by Force or Stealth: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that a financier's contractual right of repossession over a hypothecated vehicle must be exercised with great circumspection, and that a contractual repossession clause cannot be treated as a licence to seize property by force, stealth or at an inappropriate hour.

case: IBBI v. Truvisory Insolvency Professionals — Section 198 IBC
headline: Section 198 IBC Cannot Condone NCLAT Appeal Delays Beyond Section 61(2) Outer Limit
summary: The NCLAT held that Section 198 IBC — empowering condonation of delays in IBBI's statutory functions — cannot be invoked to condone delays in filing NCLAT appeals beyond the Section 61(2) outer limit of 45 days. The IBBI's 103-day delay was held un-condonable. The NCLAT is a creature of statute and cannot assume equitable jurisdiction.

case: Catalyst Trusteeship v. Ecstasy Realty — ₹600 Crore Insolvency
headline: Informal Restructuring Negotiations Cannot Override Binding Debenture Trust Deed Obligations
summary: The Supreme Court set aside NCLT/NCLAT rulings that had rejected Catalyst Trusteeship's Section 7 IBC petition on grounds of ongoing restructuring negotiations, restoring the ₹600 crore CIRP. Informal restructuring talks cannot override binding contractual obligations under a Debenture Trust Deed. Tribunal findings based on speculation and assumptions were described as perverse.

case: SBI v. Pallabh Bhowmick — Unauthorised Digital Transactions
headline: Bank Fully Liable for Unauthorised Digital Transactions Where Its Own Technology Safeguards Failed
summary: The Supreme Court upheld that a bank bears full liability for unauthorised digital transactions where the breach occurred due to the bank's own technology failure — not customer negligence. The RBI Circular of July 6, 2017 imposes zero liability on account holders in such cases. The Court rejected the bank's attempt to attribute losses to customer OTP sharing where the bank's authentication layer had already failed.

case: PayU Payments Pvt. Ltd. v. Visa Worldwide Pte. Ltd., Yes Bank, ICICI Bank & Ors.

summary: PayU challenged acquiring banks' and Visa's deductions aggregating Rs. 68.82 crore from its settlement amounts as Interchange Reimbursement Fee (IRF), arising from a dispute over merchant category code classification, and questioned the validity of Visa's private IRF compliance mechanism under Section 24 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. case: In Vogue Creations v. State Bank of India

summary: Acting Chief Justice Ravindra V. Ghuge and Justice Gautam A. Ankhad allowed a writ petition directing SBI to compensate a borrower at Rs. 5,000 per day for the bank's admitted loss of original title documents deposited as loan security, running from 1 December 2023 until the bank provides certified copies and reconstructs the title record. case: Procure Logistics Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd.
headline: A Bank Cannot Cite Generalised Suspicion to Refuse Demonetised Deposits Into a KYC-Compliant Account: NCDRC
summary: Holding Axis Bank liable for deficiency in service, the NCDRC found that the bank's blanket refusal to accept demonetised currency deposits into a KYC-compliant current account, within the window the Government's November 2016 notification allowed, was not authorised by that notification, and directed the bank to pay the complainant Rs. 3.19 crore with 6% simple interest from December 2016.

case: M/s Kabra and Associates v. Rekha & Raj Kumar Hemadev
headline: Homebuyers Cannot Switch From RERA to a Consumer Forum for the Same Grievance
summary: The Supreme Court held that once a homebuyer elects to proceed under RERA for a possession-delay grievance, the doctrine of election bars a subsequent approach to the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission for compensation on the identical cause of action. The Court set aside the NCDRC's order entertaining a parallel claim after RERA proceedings had already been invoked.

case: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Naresh Sharma — RERA Office Relocation Appeal
headline: SC Sharply Criticises RERA's Functioning, Says It May Be 'Better to Abolish' the Regulator
summary: Hearing an appeal on the relocation of the Himachal Pradesh RERA office, a bench led by the CJI observed that RERA appears to serve builders more than homebuyers, and remarked that it may be better to abolish the regulator altogether if it continues to fail in protecting consumer interests — echoing 2025 observations that RERA's functioning was "disappointing." case: Sanket Bhadresh Modi v. CBI — Digital Forensics
headline: Article 20(3) Protects Accused From Being Compelled to Disclose Digital Device Passwords
summary: The Delhi High Court held that an accused cannot be coerced by investigative agencies to disclose passwords, PINs, or access credentials for digital devices. The right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) of the Constitution extends to compelled digital disclosure — investigators cannot use contempt or legal compulsion to obtain device access from the accused.

case: Abhishek Reddy Gujjala v. M/S Ozone Urbana Infra — CMP/00754/2024
headline: Karnataka RERA Orders Full Refund With Interest for Delayed Possession Under Section 18 RERA
summary: Karnataka RERA ordered a developer to refund homebuyers with interest for delayed possession of a plot in the 'Southend' project, applying the unconditional refund right under Section 18 of the RERA Act. The ruling reinforces that any delay beyond the agreed possession date triggers the absolute right to seek a refund — without needing to establish the developer's fault or cause of delay.

case: M/s Avon Elastomers v. M/s Bajaj Allianz General Insurance and Ors.
headline: Supreme Court Flags Anomalies in How Consumer Fora's Pecuniary Jurisdiction Is Fixed
summary: Justices K.V. Viswanathan and Arun Palli questioned why consumer fora's pecuniary jurisdiction is fixed by the value of goods/services paid rather than the compensation claimed, and directed the Union to explain the basis for reducing the National Commission's jurisdiction from Rs. 10 crore to Rs. 2 crore by a December 2021 notification. Listed for further hearing on 8 October 2026.

Pancholi, issued notice on petitions challenging Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 - which amended Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act to create a blanket exemption for personal information - along with a related challenge to Section 36 of the DPDP Act and Rule 23 of the DPDP Rules empowering

case: Nikhil Mehta & Anr. v. Gardenview Abode Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.

summary: A Bench of President Justice A.P. case: Tirupati Devi Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s Raja Construction Company & Ors.

summary: A Bench of President Justice A.P. Sahi and Member Bharatkumar Pandya held that a builder's handing over of possession without obtaining the Occupation Certificate, and constructing beyond the sanctioned plan, constitutes a continuing deficiency in service, in a nearly two-decade-old Mumbai redevelopment dispute. case: Pradip Sonavane & Anr. v. DSSD Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.

summary: The complainants took possession of their redeveloped flat in the 'Shri Nandadeep Bhavan' project in 2016 but filed their consumer complaint against the developer and housing society only in 2026, alleging deficiency of service discovered later. case: Consumer Association of Buyers v. Regal Retail Marketplace Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
headline: An E-Commerce Marketplace Cannot Deflect All Liability to a Third-Party Seller Where It Controls Payment and Tracking: NCDRC
summary: Examining a marketplace platform's liability for a seller's non-delivery of paid orders, the National Commission held that a platform which collects payment, controls order-tracking, and administers refunds through its own systems cannot escape deficiency-in-service liability merely by describing itself as an intermediary connecting buyers with independent sellers.

case: Residents' Welfare Consumer Forum v. Uniform Services Contractor Pvt. Ltd.
headline: A Registered Consumer Association Can File a Complaint on Behalf of a Group of Affected Consumers: NCDRC
summary: The National Commission reaffirmed that a registered voluntary consumer association can file a complaint on behalf of one or more consumers with a common interest in the subject matter, without each individual affected consumer being separately impleaded, provided the association itself meets the statutory registration requirement.

case: Fortune Resources and Properties LLP v. Y.P. Goel and Associates and Anr.
headline: Absence of a Written Allotment Agreement Does Not Oust RERA's Jurisdiction: Chhattisgarh High Court
summary: Dismissing a builder's appeal under Section 58 of RERA, the Court held that an 'aggrieved person' under Section 31 of the Act and Rule 35 is of wide amplitude, and the mere absence of a written allotment agreement does not by itself defeat RERA's jurisdiction over a complaint, even where the underlying booking was oral.

case: Limitation for Declaration vs. Possession Suits
headline: Limitation for a Suit for Mere Declaration of Title Differs From a Suit Also Seeking Possession
summary: Courts continue to distinguish, for limitation purposes, between a suit for a bare declaration of title under Article 58 of the Limitation Act (generally three years from when the right to sue first accrues) and a suit that also seeks possession, which more commonly falls under Article 65 (twelve years) where the claim is founded on title against a party in adverse possession.

case: Neumec Developers and Builders v. Homebuyers (Second Appeals)
headline: RERA Pre-Deposit Cannot Be Dispensed With Just Because the Appeal Also Seeks Condonation of Delay
summary: Justice N.J. Jamadar dismissed two second appeals filed by Neumec Developers, holding that a promoter cannot have its delay-condonation application considered without first making the mandatory pre-deposit under Section 43(5) of RERA — a delay application is part of the appeal itself, not a separate, independent application.

summary: A Bench of Chairperson Justice J.M. Khazi and Judicial Member Santhosh Kumar Shetty N. dismissed a builder's appeal and upheld an order directing the builder and landowner to jointly pay Rs. 6 lakh as compensation to two homebuyers for construction defects, plus Rs. 5,000 in costs. case: M/s Aliens Developers Private Limited v. Telangana Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Anr.

headline: Cancelling a Flat Booking Doesn't End Your 'Allottee' Status Until You're Actually Refunded: Telangana REAT
summary: A Bench of Chairperson Justice A. Santhosh Reddy, Judicial Member P. Pradeep Kumar Reddy and Administrative Member Vemula Sreekar upheld a Telangana RERA order directing Aliens Developers to refund the balance amount due to a homebuyer who had voluntarily cancelled her flat booking, holding that execution of a cancellation deed does not by itself terminate the buyer's status as an 'allottee' - that status continues u

case: M/s Aims Max Gardenia Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. Mrs. Pratibha Gupta
headline: A 721-Day Unexplained Delay Doesn't Get Condoned, and Builders Pay Their Own Agreement's Interest Rate: Allahabad High Court
summary: The Allahabad High Court dismissed a builder's appeal seeking condonation of a 721-day delay in filing, holding that unexplained inaction and oversight do not amount to 'sufficient cause,' and upheld the RERA authority's order directing immediate possession of a Sector-75 Noida flat to the homebuyer with interest at 24% per annum (the same rate the builder-buyer agreement itself prescribed against a defaulting buyer)

case: Raintree Boulevard Apartment Owners Association v. L&T Realty Developers Ltd.
headline: Two-Thirds Allottee Consent Is Only Required Beyond What the Agreement for Sale Already Permits
summary: The Association, representing owners in the Raintree Boulevard development at Byatarayanapura, Bengaluru, sought revocation of the registration of L&T Realty's Elara Celestia project and demolition of commercial buildings, alleging modifications were made without the two-thirds allottee consent required under Section 14(2)(ii) of RERA. K-RERA, comprising Chairman Rakesh Singh and Member G.R. Reddy, dismissed the comp

case: [Homebuyer] v. BPTP Ltd. (Park Spacio, Sector 37D, Gurugram)
headline: Demanding Maintenance Charges Before Handing Over Possession Is an Unfair Trade Practice
summary: BPTP had collected Rs. 1,16,545 in maintenance charges from a homebuyer in its Park Spacio project before handing over physical possession, and had withheld possession despite full payment of the sale consideration; the builder-buyer agreement contained no clause authorising advance maintenance collection. case: Sobha Ltd. & Anr. v. Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Anr.
headline: A Promoter Can't Escape Delay Compensation by Blaming the Landowner for a Title Dispute: Karnataka Real Estate Appellate Tribunal
summary: In an appeal arising from allottee complaints over possession delay, the Karnataka Real Estate Appellate Tribunal held that a promoter cannot absolve itself of liability to pay delay compensation to an allottee merely on the ground that a landowner is internally responsible for a title issue that caused the delay. The Tribunal held that a homebuyer is protected under the RERA framework regardless of which party — the

case: Renney Geo Varghese & Anr. v. Kerala Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
headline: RERA Can't Decide a Complaint's Merits Before It's Even Numbered, or Without a Hearing: Kerala HC
summary: Ruling on a batch of two writ petitions, Justice Ziyad Rahman A.A. quashed Kerala RERA orders that had rejected the complaints of Renney Geo Varghese and Sindhu M. Poduval at the preliminary stage of scrutiny and numbering. The Court held that K-RERA's own Regulations 8 to 10 permit scrutiny only of filing requirements and accompanying documents at that stage, not adjudication of a complaint's substantive maintainabi

case: M/s Neumec Developers and Builders v. Chirag Jain & Anr.
headline: No Delay-Condonation Without the Pre-Deposit First — a RERA Appeal's Two Conditions Aren't Severable: Bombay HC
summary: Justice N.J. Jamadar dismissed two second appeals filed by promoter Neumec Developers and Builders against homebuyer-allottees, upholding the Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal's direction that the promoter could not have its application for condonation of delay in filing an appeal considered without first making the mandatory pre-deposit required under the proviso to Section 43(5) of RERA. case: Vasavi Realtors LLP v. Telangana Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
headline: RERA Registration Extension Does Not Extend the Possession Date Already Agreed With Homebuyers: Telangana REAT
summary: Dismissing 31 appeals by Vasavi Realtors against Telangana RERA orders in its 'Vasavi Lake City-West' project, a Bench of Chairperson Justice A. Santhosh Reddy, Judicial Member P. case: M/s Kabra and Associates v. Rekha Rajkumar Hemdev & Ors.
headline: A Homebuyer Who Elects the RERA Route Cannot Later Switch to the Consumer Forum on the Same Grievance: Supreme Court
summary: Setting aside an NCDRC order, the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of election of remedies, holding that homebuyers who had first approached the RERA Authority over a possession-delay grievance, and withdrawn that complaint on terms reserving liberty to refile before the same Authority, could not thereafter pursue the identical grievance before the consumer forum.

case: Jyoti Sharma v. Vishnu Goyal
headline: A Tenant's Possession Is Inherently Permissive and Can Never Ripen Into Ownership by Adverse Possession Against the Landlord
summary: The Supreme Court held that a tenant's possession, deriving as it does from the landlord's consent, cannot satisfy the hostile-possession requirement for a claim of ownership by adverse possession, regardless of how many decades the tenancy has continued or how many generations of the tenant's family have occupied the premises.

case: SEBI v. Religare Enterprises Ltd., Rashmi Saluja & Ors.
headline: SEBI Closes Non-Cooperation Proceedings Against Religare and Former Chairperson Over Burman Open Offer
summary: SEBI closed proceedings against Religare Enterprises Ltd., its former Executive Chairperson Rashmi Saluja, and five directors over their alleged failure to cooperate with the Burman Group's open offer for the company — bringing an end to one of the more closely watched open-offer compliance disputes of the year, without a finding of continued non-cooperation against the respondents.

case: SEBI v. Arshad Warsi — Social Media Pump-and-Dump
headline: SEBI Bans Actor Arshad Warsi for Social Media-Driven Securities Market Manipulation
summary: SEBI issued a prohibitory order against actor Arshad Warsi and related parties following an investigation into pump-and-dump manipulation of small-cap listed companies through social media influencer networks. The order marks a significant extension of SEBI's PFUTP enforcement into social media-driven market manipulation.

case: IMAX Corp v. E-City Entertainment
headline: Corporate Veil Pierced at Award Enforcement Stage to Implead Related Beneficiary Entities
summary: The Bombay High Court held that where an affiliate or related entity benefited from a contract subject to an arbitral award, non-parties to the arbitration may be impleaded at the enforcement stage by piercing the corporate veil. Evasion of legal obligations through separate corporate structures is not permitted.

case: Escientia Life Sciences v. Escientia Advanced Sciences
headline: NCLT Directs Structured Buy-Out for 50:50 JV Shareholder Deadlock Under Sections 241–242
summary: The NCLT directed a structured buy-out mechanism under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to resolve a shareholder deadlock in a 50:50 JV, ordering the majority shareholder to acquire the minority's shares at fair value determined by an independent valuer. The tribunal preferred judicially supervised commercial resolution over winding up.

case: National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Co-location & Dark Fibre Settlement)
headline: Supreme Court Approves NSE-SEBI's Rs. 1,491 Crore Settlement, Closing the Decade-Old Co-Location Case
summary: The Supreme Court permitted a settlement between NSE and SEBI in the decade-old algorithmic-trading co-location and dark-fibre cases, under which NSE will pay approximately Rs. 1,491.21 crore under SEBI's settlement mechanism (Rs. 1,223.56 crore for co-location and Rs. 267.65 crore for the dark-fibre matter), disposing of SEBI's pending appeals against the Securities Appellate Tribunal's 2023 order that had earlier s

case: Nikhil Rai & Anr. v. VCare Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
headline: A Commercial Justification for Restructuring Doesn't Dispense With the NCLT's Duty to Examine an Oppression Petition: NCLAT
summary: The NCLT had dismissed a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement after the respondents defended the impugned restructuring as commercially necessary. A Bench of Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Arun Baroka and Indevar Pandey set aside that dismissal and remanded the matter, holding that a respondent's detailed commercial justification for a restructuring does not by itself dispense with the adjudicating authority'

case: Srideva Sattva Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana
headline: GST Proceedings Vitiated Where There Is No Material Showing the Show-Cause Notice Was Actually Served: Supreme Court
summary: The Supreme Court held that where there is no material on record establishing service of the show-cause notice on the assessee, the proceedings culminating in an ex parte order-in-original are vitiated for breach of natural justice, reinforcing that a GST department cannot rely on an assumption of service without a documented record.

case: Union of India v. Gujarat Chamber of Commerce and Industry
headline: Supreme Court Declines to Interfere With Gujarat HC Ruling That Assignment of GIDC Leasehold Rights Is Not Exigible to GST
summary: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the Gujarat High Court's judgment holding that assignment of leasehold rights allotted by the Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation does not attract GST, treating the assignment as a transfer of an existing interest in immovable property rather than a fresh supply of service.

case: Koenig Solutions Pvt. Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner, Audit Branch
headline: A GST Special Audit Can't Stay Open Once the Underlying Demand Order's Deadline Has Passed: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court quashed a special-audit communication issued in Form GST ADT-03 and a consequential DRC-01 against Koenig Solutions for FY 2018-19, after the GST department conceded that no final order under Section 73 of the CGST Act had been passed by the statutory deadline of 30 April 2024. case: Spherion Solutions Private Limited v. Additional Commissioner, Adjudication, CGST Delhi North & Ors.
headline: ITC Blocked Under Rule 86A Cannot Be Used to Satisfy a GST Appeal's Pre-Deposit: Delhi High Court
summary: A Bench of Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain held that Input Tax Credit blocked under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules cannot itself satisfy the mandatory pre-deposit required under Section 107(6) of the CGST Act to file a GST appeal, since a Rule 86A restriction prevents the credit from being debited from the electronic credit ledger unless the restriction is first removed or modified by the competent authority.
